source.title: AdaCap: Adaptive Capacity control for Feed-Forward Neural Networks
source.authors: K. Meziani; Karim Lounici; Benjamin Riu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff affecting the relevant sections.
record.tranche_reason: The paper’s own results and arguments refine the regularization claim: AdaCap uses randomly permuted labels as a training signal to delay memorization, and explicitly states ordinary regularizers cannot prevent memorization. It does not directly reproduce the original random-label fitting experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2016) and Arpit et al. (2017) for random-label memorization as prior work; those cited results are not rows. Its own relevant results concern AdaCap’s behavior and comparisons with ordinary DNN regularization on tabular data. Numeric accuracy and loss values from the AdaCap benchmarks do not measure the versions’ specified random-label fit, noisy-label degradation, or learning order.
record.test_reason: AdaCap uses randomly permuted labels to construct a capacity-control objective and evaluates generalization performance. It does not report standard networks' fit to random labels, corruption-dependent convergence, or real-versus-noisy label learning order. The introductory statement about ordinary regularizers failing to prevent memorization cites Arpit et al.; it is not an independent result or specific argument testing V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that combining the MLR loss with the Tikhonov operator controls FFNN capacity and changes learning dynamics. They report strong regression results, especially on high-SNR tabular datasets, poor binary classification results, and promising preliminary CNN results on MNIST.
record.recipe_differences: AdaCap is a proposed capacity-control training method using Tikhonov regularization and a MLR objective, evaluated chiefly on tabular generalization; it is not a reproduction of the original random-label memorization experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that AdaCap's effectiveness depends on task and architecture: it is nearly irrelevant for classification but usually improves regression, especially high-SNR regression; it does not combine well with dropout or batch normalization in the reported ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 reports altered training and validation RMSE dynamics on Abalone under Tikhonov and AdaCap, interpreted as delayed memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive capacity control can change learning dynamics and improve validation performance on ordinary tabular regression data.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 2.1 and Figure 4 examine a permuted-label criterion as a generalization-risk estimator for ridge regression under specified signal-to-noise conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Permuted labels can help estimate generalization risk and select ridge regularization strength.

record.problems: No direct random-label fitting study of standard networks; the random-label claims from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are cited prior work, not results from this study. The paper's empirical focus is tabular data, and it reports AdaCap underperforms regular DNNs on classification.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible rows. Benchmark RMSE, classification results, and AdaCap learning-dynamic plots do not directly measure any listed version's specified random-label behavior. Figure 2 describes AdaCap's own train/validation RMSE dynamics on Abalone, not fitting random labels with standard networks.

untested.parts: Random-label training error and chance-level test performance in standard networks with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus true labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Perfect training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across random label-corruption fractions.

Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing explicit regularization alone preserves true-label generalization. AdaCap comparisons change the training objective and capacity-control scheme, so they do not isolate removal alone.
Direct comparison of learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: The empty row set is appropriate. Correct the record's T5 classification and V5 tested status: neither the cited introductory assertion nor AdaCap's benchmark performance establishes a test of any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No direct experiment tests standard networks trained on completely random labels for training error, test error, or unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
No comparison measures training time to fit true versus random labels or convergence as corruption increases.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise-input experiment.
No sweep of random label-corruption fractions reporting training fit and test error.

The text explicitly argues common regularizers cannot prevent memorization, but supplies no result measuring whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels, nor whether removing them alone worsens generalization.
No experiment tests the ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noisy or random labels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
